title: Defeated, then victorious
hook: the Romans have been defeated, and within a few years will win (30:2–4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-'ankabut, the spider whose house can't hold. Your line was not the spider's house. Today, a new surah.

News of a far-off war reaches Mecca. Two empires are fighting: the Romans of Constantinople, whom historians now call the Byzantines, and the Persians. The Romans are losing. In Mecca, far from the fighting, people take sides. A report in Tirmidhi says the Muslims wanted the Romans to win, since they were people of a scripture, and the Quraysh wanted the Persians, who, like them, had no scripture. Then a surah opens with a headline.

Surah Ar-Rum, the Romans, the thirtieth. Pickthall: "The Romans have been defeated". In the nearer land, the verses go on, and after their defeat they will be victorious, within a few years. The phrase is bid' sinin. Bid' means a handful, a small number; the same report in Tirmidhi gives it as between three and nine. And on that day the believers will rejoice in God's help. The Quraysh laughed. The report says Abu Bakr was so sure that he made a wager with some of them, before wagers like that were forbidden, and when the Romans won, he won it. Tradition says the emperor Heraclius turned the war. Some commentators link the believers' rejoicing to the same season as their own victory at Badr; others read it differently, and scholars have discussed exactly which events fit. But the verses don't stay with empires. The next lines say: God's is the command, before and after. Then the surah widens into a long meditation on signs: night and day, rain on dead earth, the cycle of life. In the surah's picture, a defeat isn't the end of a story. It's a chapter. The defeated can win within a handful of years, and the One who turns it is the One who brings green out of dead ground.
screen: `THE ROMANS HAVE BEEN DEFEATED.` · `BID' SININ: A HANDFUL OF YEARS.` · `ABU BAKR'S WAGER.` · `GOD'S IS THE COMMAND, BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you're losing right now: your health, a project that keeps failing, a relationship gone cold, a habit that keeps winning. Don't pretend it isn't a defeat; hold it, then imagine the same scene a handful of years from now, turned around, and notice what small step points that way. If you pray, you can ask for help with it.
Defeated. The opening of Ar-Rum: the Romans have been defeated, and after their defeat they will win, within a handful of years. Today's word.
Your line: within a few years. The command is God's, before and after. That's day five hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Muslims read the opening of Surah Ar-Rum as a prophecy fulfilled in the Byzantine recovery under Heraclius, and as a reminder that the outcome of events belongs to God.

chat.says: What's the story behind the opening of Surah Ar-Rum?
options: The Romans had been defeated, and the verses said they'd win within a few years.
The Muslims had lost a battle, and the verses promised them revenge.
Rome had just conquered Mecca, and the surah calls for resistance.
chat.meaning: 30:2–4: the Romans have been defeated, and after their defeat they will be victorious within bid' sinin, a handful of years.

bid' sinin.meaning: a handful of years, a few years

Heraclius.meaning: the Roman emperor who, tradition says, turned the war

Badr.meaning: a battle the early Muslims won

sources.ref: Qur'an 30:3–5 (victory within a few years; God's command)

notes: Pickthall 30:2 quoted from memory; confirm. Pickthall renders bid' sinin in 30:4 as 'within ten years', I believe; the script paraphrases with 'within a few years', matching the outline. Confirm.
Abu Bakr's wager: Tirmidhi 3193 cited from memory; confirm. The note 'before wagers like that were forbidden' follows the commentaries.
Some commentators tie the believers' rejoicing to Badr (624), others to Hudaybiyyah or to the Roman victory itself; script says 'read both ways'. Confirm.
